disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more persistent, non-bizarre or minimally bizarre delusions lasting at least one month in a person whose overall functioning is relatively preserved and whose behavior is not obviously odd or markedly disorganized outside the delusional context. Aside from the delusional beliefs, mood and thought processes are often relatively intact, and criteria for schizophrenia (such as prominent hallucinations, disorganized speech, or negative symptoms) are not met. Onset is typically in mid to late adulthood and may be associated with psychosocial stressors, social isolation, sensory impairment, or personality traits such as suspiciousness or rigidity. The course is usually chronic, with beliefs that remain fixed despite clear contradictory evidence, and individuals may only come to clinical attention when interpersonal conflict, legal problems, or functional decline arise directly from their delusional convictions.

narrative.personality: Keegan is a meticulous, curiosity-driven and community-minded woodworker who tends to plan carefully, take responsibility for others, and sometimes overextends himself in volunteer roles.
narrative.stressor: Over the past two years, Keegan’s part-time woodworking business slowed significantly as cheaper, mass-produced furniture undercut his custom pieces, and a key arts grant for the community festivals he coordinated was suddenly denied after what he perceived as a flawless application. Already detail-oriented and vigilant about finances and health, he began poring obsessively over correspondence with the grant committee and former clients, trying to understand why opportunities kept slipping away. As months passed, he withdrew more into his garage workshop and late-night research, increasingly interpreting ambiguous events in the arts community as targeted actions against his projects, while his wife and colleagues noticed he was harder to collaborate with on festivals. After nearly a year of escalating tension with local arts boards and strained conversations at home about his insistence on a specific hidden cause for his setbacks, his spouse and a long-time collaborator persuaded him to see a psychiatrist to help him "get a reality check" about the fixed explanations he had developed.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m here because everyone keeps telling me these beliefs I have about what’s going on aren’t realistic, but they feel completely true to me no matter what they show me.”

narrative.personality: Ulisses is a socially engaged, organized, and ambitious student-leader who thrives on coordinating events, helping his community, and staying deeply involved with friends and soccer.
narrative.stressor: In his first year of college, Ulisses threw himself into campus leadership, community activism, and coordinating local soccer tournaments while juggling classes and commuting from home, leaving little downtime and mounting pressure to perform. After a contentious student election and a dispute over field permits for a tournament he helped organize, he felt unfairly blamed and began replaying email threads and group chats, convinced that certain peers were working against him behind the scenes. Over the following months, he became increasingly preoccupied with interpreting routine scheduling changes, social media posts, and minor setbacks as part of a coordinated effort, even as he maintained his grades and continued volunteering. Friends and a trusted faculty advisor, worried by how rigidly he held to this specific narrative despite reassurances and evidence to the contrary, encouraged him to see a mental health professional when organizing even small events started to revolve around his attempts to anticipate and counter these perceived machinations.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep getting stuck on certain ideas about what people are really doing, and no matter what anyone says, I can’t shake these beliefs.”

narrative.personality: Malcolm is an outgoing, creative, and community-oriented designer who thrives on collaboration and social energy but often overcommits to projects and nightlife at the expense of rest.
narrative.stressor: About a year ago, Malcolm hit a rough patch when a major branding contract he’d invested months of work into was abruptly canceled after internal changes at the client company, followed closely by critical online feedback on one of his public design installations. Proud of his self-taught trajectory and sensitive to professional respect, he began to brood over the cancellations and comments, combing through design forums and social media, and gradually came to feel that specific industry peers were taking ideas from him and subtly undermining his reputation. Over the ensuing months, he became more guarded in workshops, less willing to share drafts, and increasingly focused on tracing supposed patterns in others’ portfolios and posts that he believed confirmed a particular, unshakeable explanation for his stalled opportunities. When collaborators started distancing themselves, citing how hard it had become to discuss feedback with him, and a close friend pointed out how much his work decisions were being driven by these fixed assumptions, Malcolm agreed—reluctantly—to seek psychiatric help to sort out why he couldn’t let go of these beliefs despite how much conflict they were causing.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m stuck on these beliefs about what people in my field are doing to my work, and even when everyone tells me I’m wrong, I just can’t see it any other way.”
